name: Lexical Sophistication (Frequency Band Profiling)
description: Evaluates the proportion of rare, highly specific, or advanced vocabulary used in the text. AI models inherently gravitate toward 'safe,' high- and mid-frequency words to maximize statistical probability, consistently avoiding the obscure, low-frequency terminology that human experts naturally employ.
algorithm: Corpus Frequency Band Mapping & AWL (Academic Word List) Penetration Scoring
mechanism: Every word in a language can be mapped to its statistical frequency of use in the real world (e.g., 'house' is high-frequency, 'defenestrate' is low-frequency). Human writers, especially experts or creative authors, draw heavily from low-frequency bands (rare words) to describe specific nuances, establish authority, or create poetic impact. Conversely, Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained using cross-entropy loss to predict the *most likely* next word. Even when instructed to write professionally, they statistically struggle to reach deep into the low-frequency bands, instead relying on the most common Academic Word List (AWL) terms and mid-frequency professional jargon. This algorithm cross-references every content word in the text against massive linguistic frequency corpora (such as SUBTLEX or BNC). It categorizes the vocabulary into frequency bands (Top 1K, 2K, 5K, 10K, and Off-List). If a text claims to be expert-level but its semantic profile is overwhelmingly dominated by the top 5,000 most common words with a conspicuous absence of 'Off-List' rare terminology, it is flagged as an artificial, probability-smoothed generation.
useCase: Crucial for analyzing academic papers, technical documentation, and high-level journalism. It effectively exposes AI-generated texts that sound superficially 'smart' but lack true specialized depth.
strengths:
• Quantifies the 'uncanny valley' of AI writing—why an LLM essay feels structurally perfect but intellectually shallow.
• Extremely difficult to bypass by simply telling the AI to 'use big words'; LLMs will just spam the most common 'complex' words (e.g., 'delve', 'tapestry', 'multifaceted') rather than using genuinely context-appropriate rare vocabulary.
• Grounded in decades of established psycholinguistic research on human vocabulary acquisition.
limitations:
• Performance plummets on texts inherently designed to be simple, such as children's books, basic instructions, or casual social media posts, which naturally use high-frequency words.
• Requires massive, highly accurate frequency dictionaries for every single supported language; English is well-supported, but minor languages may lack the necessary corpora.
• Technical texts in extremely niche domains might introduce specific jargon that skews the off-list word count, requiring domain-specific calibration.
parameters:
Analysis: Linguistic Corpus Cross-Referencing
Metric: Proportion of Low-Frequency vs. High-Frequency Vocabulary
Output: 0-100 Lexical Predictability (Vocabulary Smoothing) Score
accuracy: High — 79-86% on academic and professional texts. It successfully captures the AI's structural inability to consistently utilize rare, expert-level terminology.

references.title: Kyle, K. & Crossley, S. A. (2015). Automatically Assessing Lexical Sophistication: Indices, Tools, Findings, and Application. TESOL Quarterly.
Kobak, D. et al. (2024). Delving into ChatGPT Usage in Academic Writing Through Excess Vocabulary. arXiv.
